nameStory: This butterfly is named after Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and beauty, reflecting its stunning orange and silver coloration. The word 'fritillary' comes from the Latin word for a dice cup, referring to the checkered pattern on the wings that resembles the spotted markings inside ancient Roman dice boxes.
description: The Aphrodite Fritillary is a medium-to-large orange butterfly with distinctive black markings and silvery spots underneath its wings. Adults have a wingspan of about 2.5 to 3.5 inches, making them quite noticeable when they flutter by. The upper wings are bright orange-brown with intricate black lines, dots, and crescents, while the underwings display beautiful metallic silver spots that catch the light. Like all fritillaries, they're strong fliers with a characteristic bouncing flight pattern.

idTips.label: Silver underwing spots
idTips.description: The hindwings underneath have large, round silvery spots that gleam like mirrors in sunlight - you can actually see your reflection in them up close

idTips.label: Orange upperwings with black markings
idTips.description: Bright pumpkin-orange wings with bold black lines, crescents, and dots that feel slightly fuzzy to the touch due to tiny scales

idTips.label: Wing border pattern
idTips.description: A narrow, unbroken black border runs along the outer edge of both forewings and hindwings, creating a clean frame

idTips.label: Body appearance
idTips.description: Robust, hairy orange body with black spots that feels surprisingly sturdy when gently handled

idTips.label: Flight behavior
idTips.description: Strong, bouncing flight pattern with quick wingbeats followed by brief glides, often flying higher than other butterflies

habitat: Look for Aphrodite Fritillaries in sunny meadows, prairies, old fields, and woodland edges throughout New England, particularly where violets grow since these are their host plants. They prefer open areas with good nectar sources like milkweed, thistle, and goldenrod, often at elevations from sea level up to about 3,000 feet. You'll frequently spot them in areas that were once farmland but are now returning to nature.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active - look for tiny caterpillars emerging from winter hiding spots among violet leaves in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time from mid-June through August when adults are most active, feeding on nectar and mating. This is the best time to observe their full beauty.
seasonality.fall: Flight continues into early September, with worn individuals still visible but showing faded colors and tattered wing edges from months of activity.
seasonality.winter: No adults present - young caterpillars overwinter in leaf litter and debris, waiting for spring violets to emerge.

funFact: Aphrodite Fritillary caterpillars are actually born in late summer but immediately go to sleep for the winter without eating a single meal - they survive eight months on just the nutrients from their egg yolk until violets appear in spring.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Great Spangled Fritillary, but Aphrodites have a narrow, unbroken black wing border while Great Spangled have a wider border that's often broken with orange spots. Memory trick: 'Aphrodite has a neat black outline like eyeliner - Great Spangled's border is messier with orange spots breaking through.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name suggesting a connection to ancient mythology, fritillary butterflies were actually named by early naturalists who were struck by their dice-cup pattern long before anyone connected this particular species to the goddess Aphrodite.
compareHints: Compared to Great Spangled Fritillary, Aphrodite is slightly smaller and has that distinctive unbroken black wing border. Atlantis Fritillary is much smaller and darker, with more muted orange coloring and different silver spot patterns underneath. The Aphrodite sits right in the middle size-wise and has the cleanest, most defined black wing borders of the three New England greater fritillaries.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relatives, the Great Spangled Fritillary is the largest and most robust of the three Argynnis species in New England.

Compared to its close relatives, the Atlantis Fritillary is smaller than the Great Spangled Fritillary and lacks the wide, unspotted pale band that the Aphrodite Fritillary shows on its hindwing underside.
